**What a ralph loop is:** Geoffrey Huntley's [Ralph Wiggum technique](https://ghuntley.com/loop/) — a dumb `while true` that re-invokes a **fresh** agent session with the same prompt every iteration. Progress accumulates in files and git history, never in the model's context window; each pass does one small task until the checklist is empty. ([history](https://www.humanlayer.dev/blog/brief-history-of-ralph), [deep dive](https://www.zerosync.co/blog/ralph-loop-technical-deep-dive), [ghuntley/how-to-ralph-wiggum](https://github.com/ghuntley/how-to-ralph-wiggum))

All right, the user wants to verify that the Ralph loop correctly detects when the opencode session limit is reached, and to fix it if it doesn't. I already attempted two probes:

1. A simple `timeout 120 opencode run ... "reply with the single word ok"` which timed out (exit code 124). That tells me the process hit the timeout, but I don't know whether opencode itself reported a quota or rate‑limit error, or if the timeout was just the shell killing the command.

2. A more detailed probe with `--print-logs --log-level INFO` that captures the full log output. The result was too large (72 KB) for the normal tool output, so the system saved it to a temporary file at  
`/home/lane/.claude/projects/-home-lane-MythosMini/5eeb7e10-99a4-4d7d-a505-3ef47dcab480/tool-results/b0cmcevm0.txt`.

Now I need to actually inspect that saved log to see what error messages opencode emitted. The user specifically asked “see if it detects it properly. if not, fix it.” So the next logical step is to extract any error identifiers, status codes, or textual hints about limits or retries from the log. Because the file is large, I should avoid dumping the whole thing; instead I’ll grep for patterns that are likely to contain the relevant info.

What patterns should I look for? Based on the preview, I see JSON‑like error objects with fields such as `"error":{...}`, `"name":"AI_APICallError"`, `"statusCode":429`, `"message":"... limit ..."` or `"retry"` strings. A robust approach is to search for:

- `"message":"...` – capture up to a reasonable length (say 200 characters) after the key.
- `name":"[A-Za-z]+"` – the error name.
- `statusCode":[0-9]+` – HTTP status codes.
- `retry` – any retry‑related text.
- `limit` – any mention of limits.

I’ll use `grep -oiE` with a regex that captures any of those fragments. The `-o` flag prints only the matching part, `-i` makes it case‑insensitive, and `-E` allows extended regex. After extracting matches, I want to see which ones appear most frequently, so I’ll pipe through `sort`, then `uniq -c` to count occurrences, then sort numerically descending, and finally `head -20` to limit to the top 20 distinct messages. This should give me a concise summary of any limit‑related errors.

Thus the command I need to run is:

```
grep -oiE '"message":"[^"]{0,200}"|name":"[A-Za-z]+"|statusCode":[0-9]+|retry[^,]{0,80}|limit[^,\"]{0,80}' \
    /home/lane/.claude/projects/-home-lane-MythosMini/5eeb7e10-99a4-4d7d-a505-3ef47dcab480/tool-results/b0cmcevm0.txt \
    | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
```

This will extract the relevant snippets, count them, and show the most common ones. Running this will let me determine whether the opencode client is reporting a quota/limit error, and then I can decide if any code changes are needed to handle it. I’ll now issue this as a Bash tool call.
